stem: Someone argues: "Frontier training runs are heading toward drawing as much electricity as a small city. Nothing like that has ever been built for one computation, so scaling will have to stop within a few years." Which response best fits the current evidence on scaling?

options.text: Runs at that scale look feasible; the open questions are whether the economic returns justify them and whether chips and power arrive in time
Runs at that scale look feasible, so continued scaling is the expected outcome and what remains is mostly engineering the physical build-out
options.provenance: drops 'The question is whether the economic incentives justify it and whether the infrastructure constraints ... can be overcome in time', reading 'they aren't impossible' as 'they will happen'

options.text: The argument holds: power and chip supply impose a physical ceiling that training runs of that size cannot realistically get past
options.provenance: misreads 'comparable to running a small city' as a ceiling, against 'These are unprecedented scales, but analysis suggests that they aren't impossible'

options.text: Power is a side issue; the binding limit is the stock of public text, which is used up well before power demand becomes decisive
options.provenance: right idea, wrong slot: promotes the Training Data subsection's data wall to the decisive constraint, when the text lists data as one infrastructure constraint among several and says whether it binds depends on the escape routes

explanation: The analysis we draw on finds city-scale training runs unprecedented but not impossible, so physical impossibility is the wrong objection. What stays open is conditional: whether the economic incentives justify spending at that scale, and whether chips, power and data can be supplied in time. If you picked the physical-ceiling option, you took the size of the number as a limit; unprecedented is not the same as unbuildable, and that is the prior this part of the section overturns. If you picked the 'expected outcome' option, you kept the feasibility finding but dropped its two conditions, and feasible-if-funded is not the same as inevitable. The data-wall option treats one constraint as decisive, when whether data binds depends on how well the escape routes work. (Forecasting Timelines)
takeaway: Not impossible is a different claim from inevitable: feasibility leaves the economics and the build-out open.

self_check.cover_test: Yes: a reader who absorbed 'not impossible, but depends on incentives and infrastructure' can state the key's two-part answer unaided.
self_check.cynic_test: A skipper might pick the confident 'feasible, so it happens' option or the sceptical ceiling; the key and top distractor share the 'look feasible' opening and length, so only the dropped conditions separate them, and 'power' appears in three options, so no word-match tell.

stem: You enter your own views on investment growth, software efficiency gains, hardware improvement and how many tasks each extra order of magnitude of compute automates into a simple forecasting model. It says full automation arrives decades earlier than you had assumed. What is the most useful thing to do with that result?

options.text: Take the mismatch as a sign that one of your inputs or your prior expectation is off, and work out which of them to revise
Take the mismatch as a sign that the model is mis-specified, and set its output aside in favour of the date you had expected
options.provenance: reverses 'If you're surprised, maybe one of your input beliefs needs updating', pointing the surprise at the model rather than at the inputs you supplied

options.text: Take the mismatch as ordinary noise, since forecast ranges are far too wide for a single model output to carry much information
options.provenance: conflates the section's 'wide error margins that compound over time' with uselessness, missing that the consistency check survives the uncertainty

options.text: Take the output as the model's prediction of the date, and judge the model later by whether automation arrives around then
options.provenance: the prior the section targets: reads forecasts as 'concrete predictions of timelines' rather than 'scenarios that help you reason about different potential futures'

explanation: A model like this is useful as a coherence check. The inputs were your own views, so an output that clashes with the date you expected means your views do not fit together: either one of the inputs is wrong, or the expectation is. Finding out which one is the point of the exercise. If you chose to judge the model later by the actual arrival date, you were treating it as a date prediction. We present forecasts as scenarios for reasoning about possible futures, and an arrival date can't tell you which of your beliefs was the odd one out. Setting the output aside because it surprised you throws away exactly the signal the check is designed to give you. Wide error bars are real, but they don't make an inconsistency between your own beliefs go away. (Forecasting Timelines)
takeaway: When a forecast built from your own inputs surprises you, the surprise points back at your beliefs, not at the model.

self_check.cover_test: Yes: a reader who understood 'if you're surprised, maybe one of your input beliefs needs updating' would say 'find which of my beliefs is inconsistent' before seeing options.
self_check.cynic_test: All four options open with the same 'Take the ... as' frame at similar length, and 'model' appears in two distractors but not the key, so a skipper can't lean on stem-word echo; the two 'humble' options (noise, discard) sound as reasonable as the key without the section.

stem: Suppose compute-based scaling laws keep holding for the next few decades. How much uncertainty would remain about when transformative AI (TAI) arrives, and why?

options.text: A lot: the laws tie compute to performance, but not to how much compute TAI needs, and estimates of that span many orders of magnitude
Little: once compute is tied to performance, arrival follows from compute trends, which are tracked closely enough to name a year
options.provenance: misreads 'Even if we assume compute-based scaling laws hold, we still don't know how much compute TAI will actually require' as saying the laws settle the timing

options.text: A lot: the compute TAI needs is pegged to the human brain, and direct measurements of the brain's compute are still too noisy to pin down
options.provenance: misreads the source of the biological-anchors spread as measurement error, when the section attributes it to which biological process is taken as the reference (lifetime learning vs evolutionary history)

options.text: Some, but a bounded amount: errors in the compute trend stay about the same size however far ahead the forecast is run
options.provenance: misses 'compound over time' in the lead 'All forecasts come with wide error margins that compound over time'

explanation: Scaling laws tell you how performance rises with compute. They don't tell you where on that curve transformative AI sits, and that is the quantity people disagree about. Biological-anchor estimates of the compute TAI requires run from what a human uses learning skills over a lifetime to everything evolution spent shaping humans, which is roughly twelve orders of magnitude. The spread comes from choosing which biological process to treat as the reference, not from noisy brain measurements, so better neuroscience instruments wouldn't close it. The 'little' option assumes that fixing the curve fixes the target. The 'bounded' option misses that errors compound: a small miss in a yearly growth rate grows with every year the projection runs. That's why a date like '2045' should be read as the rough centre of a wide range. (Forecasting Timelines)
takeaway: Scaling laws give you the curve, not the finish line; the uncertainty about how much compute TAI needs survives even if the laws hold perfectly.

self_check.cover_test: Yes: 'even if scaling laws hold we don't know how much compute TAI requires, and anchors span orders of magnitude' is a sentence a reader of the section can produce unaided.
self_check.cynic_test: A skipper might pick either 'A lot' option by the section's obvious uncertainty theme, but the noisy-measurement option also says 'A lot' and names the brain, so the choice turns on knowing the spread comes from the reference process; 'TAI' and 'compute' appear in several options, so they are not a word-match tell.

note: Misconception lens applied to all three ideas. FT-2 and FT-3 are a discrimination_pairs entry, but I kept them as separate candidates: each started from its own misconception (surprise means the model is wrong; the laws settle the timing), and the pair's 'error bars make it worthless' conflation appears as a family-(a) distractor in f02. FT-3 uses 'many orders of magnitude' only in the key's wording, not as a number, so the width is not a load-bearing figure and the R11 budget stays unspent. The FT-10 stem leaves out the 2030 date and the dollar and gigawatt figures, so nothing volatile is load-bearing.
